prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the case on the table where a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, with flat bands at a magic angle) was matched by nature, and where the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018 then created a whole field, moire quantum materials, with a single tunable control parameter. It is a discovery rather than a construction, it is robustly reproduced by many independent groups across several moire platforms, and the theory-plus-experiment split gives a natural three-person configuration within the supplied names. Five of the eight opening ballots put it first or second, and six put it in the top three, but I rest the case on the science: originality, a prediction confirmed, and very large downstream impact.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution and maturity. Earlier twisted-graphene theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) anticipated the band flattening, and the experimental first author, Yuan Cao, and other moire groups are outside the credited set, so a three-name prize will look contested. The pairing mechanism of the superconducting state is also unresolved, which may make the citation awkward and make some colleagues feel the field is still young; there is a risk that we honour a platform whose deepest physics is not yet understood.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery (B016) first as a genuinely novel instrument opening a new window on cosmic-ray accelerators, with the diffuse flux confirmed in several channels.
responses.response: I agree that this is a real discovery from nature and I ranked it third myself. My reservation is attribution and maturity: a collaboration of this size makes it hard to defend two names, and, as you note, individual source identification is still at modest significance, so the prize would effectively rest on the diffuse flux while the origin of most of it is unknown. I would hold it as a strong alternative or a later-year candidate rather than prefer it over a case where both prediction and observation are clean. I would like to hear how you would phrase a citation that is not tied to a particular source.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory (B037) first as a standard, mature non-perturbative framework for correlated electrons, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second, noting the pairing mechanism and phase diagram are unsettled.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously: DMFT has two decades of validation and wide use, and the open pairing question in twisted bilayer graphene is real. But DMFT is a method, and its credit problem is acute, since Metzner, whose infinite-dimension limit made it possible, is outside the supplied names, as you yourself say. Twisted bilayer graphene is a discovery of a new regime of matter that others then reproduced, and its core observations do not depend on the pairing mechanism being settled. I do not think an unresolved mechanism should disqualify a discovery; the 2016 prize also honoured phases whose full understanding was still developing.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B045) first, as a mature, independently confirmed advance with 1e-18 accuracy and a likely redefinition of the second, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene outside his top eight.
responses.response: I find the lattice-clock case strong on maturity and attribution, and Katori plus Ye is cleaner than my three-name configuration. My disagreement is about what we are rewarding: it is an extraordinary measurement advance, but it sits after the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes and is closer to an engineering achievement in precision than to a new phenomenon. I would be persuaded if the committee judges that tests of relativity and constants with these clocks are the discovery. I therefore keep it as my first alternative, not my preference.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B026) first and trapped ions (B007) second as foundational, mature quantum-technology platforms, and places twisted bilayer graphene sixth.
responses.response: Circuit QED is a clean theory-plus-experiment trio and I agree it is mature, which is why it is my second alternative. My concern is timing and framing: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a close sequel look repetitive, and much of its impact is as an architecture for devices, which sits nearer invention than discovery. Twisted bilayer graphene has no recent prize overlap on the physics itself, so I think it has the stronger claim this year, though I accept that you weigh the quantum-technology impact more heavily than I do.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a three-name set that excludes early twisted-graphene theorists and the experimental first author, or whether this makes the case premature.
Whether the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism should affect the citation wording or the timing.
How much weight 2025 prize overlap should carry against circuit QED, and the 2016 topological-phase prize against the topological-insulator candidates.
My recollection of the detailed priority history of twisted-bilayer theory comes from general knowledge and is not verified from the supplied files.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of the credited names for the shortlisted candidates is among my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group), and my own work in string theory and cosmology is not in this area.
